\title{Adapting ECG-FM for Chagas screening under a recording-length shortcut: internal evidence and hidden-cohort scores from the PhysioNet Challenge 2025}

\keywords{Chagas disease, electrocardiogram, foundation model, fine-tuning, shortcut learning, PhysioNet Challenge, generalisation}


\begin{abstract}
\textit{Objective.} Our entry to the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025 detected Chagas disease from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) with the ECG-FM foundation model kept frozen. We asked whether fine-tuning the encoder would do better, and how to judge that on the public data.
\textit{Approach.} We added one change at a time to the entry: soft labels, augmentation, two-stage fine-tuning with layer-wise learning-rate decay, unpadded windows of ECG-FM's pretraining length, a hard-negative ranking loss and seed ensembling. Models were compared on a patient-grouped held-out split, within recording length, under rules written before each round.
\textit{Main results.} In CODE-15\%, the largest training source, short records are \prevRatio{} times as often positive as long ones, and record length alone reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of \durOnlyB. Every model trained on padded 10 s inputs scored short negatives higher than long ones; pretraining-length windows and the ranking loss together reduced that gap in mean probability from \rThreeBzGap{} to \rThreeWoneRGap. Unfreezing the transformer layers improved the true positive rate among the top 5\% of records (\tpr) over the frozen-encoder head it started from (\mwSseven{} vs \frozenSseven), but we could not show that it beats a frozen encoder trained to convergence. On the organisers' hidden test cohorts, the revised entry raised our score from \extOrigMean{} to \extNewMean; a one-day hackathon variant scored \extHackMean.
\textit{Significance.} A short second stage of fine-tuning improved on the initial frozen-encoder checkpoint. On these data, changes could be judged only within recording length.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Chagas disease, caused by \textit{Trypanosoma cruzi}, affects millions of people in Latin America and is often silent for decades before it produces cardiomyopathy. Serological testing is the diagnostic standard but capacity is limited, so an inexpensive test that ranks people for serology is valuable. The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is a natural candidate, because Chagas cardiomyopathy leaves conduction and rhythm abnormalities such as right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block \citep{jidling2023}.

The George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025 asked teams to rank ECGs by the probability of Chagas disease \citep{reyna2025,goldberger2000}. The score is the true positive rate among the 5\% of records with the highest predicted probability (\tpr), that is, the fraction of all positive cases found there. Training data came from three public sources with labels of very different quality: CODE-15\% with self-reported labels \citep{ribeiro2020}, SaMi-Trop with serologically confirmed positives \citep{cardoso2016}, and PTB-XL with presumed negatives \citep{wagner2020}. Models were scored on three hidden, serologically labelled Brazilian cohorts.

Several strong entries started from a pretrained ECG encoder, and they did not agree on whether to fine-tune it. The winning team found full fine-tuning of its vision-transformer foundation model better than a head on the frozen model, with a cross-validated score of 0.490 against 0.381 \citep{vansantvliet2025}. Another team, whose encoders were pretrained on CODE-15\%, found that its SEResNet18 encoder scored higher on the hidden validation cohort when frozen than when fine-tuned (0.338 against 0.231), although for its other encoder fine-tuning with feature distillation beat freezing \citep{wang2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against vansantvliet2025 (CV 0.490 full fine-tuning vs 0.381 frozen backbone, results section) and wang2025 (table 1).
With noisy labels, fine-tuning could degrade pretrained features or improve their sensitivity to disease-associated ECG features.

Our entry kept the ECG-FM encoder \citep{mckeen2025} frozen and trained a small head on its output, with age and sex concatenated to the pooled feature \citep{nguyen2025}. It scored \extOrigMean{} on the hidden test set, eighth of the ranked teams.
% verified 2026-11-12 against the official results table (rank 8, test 0.245). No denominator: the table has 39 numeric ranks (1-40 with ties), the CinC abstract says 40 and Reyna et al say 41.
Internally, unfreezing the encoder had cost us 0.08 of score, and our internal and hidden scores disagreed: a model that scored among the best on our own split, trained without CODE-15\%, scored 0.081 on the hidden validation cohort.
% verified 2026-11-12 against nguyen2025, table 3 (unfrozen/BCE 0.342 vs frozen/BCE 0.426; k-fold without CODE-15% 0.534 internal, 0.081 hidden validation, against 0.323; an SE model scored 0.540 internally and 0.079 on hidden validation).
Disagreement of this kind suggests that a model has learned a feature that predicts the label in the training data but is unrelated to the disease, that is, a \emph{shortcut} \citep{geirhos2020}. In medical imaging, shortcuts have been traced to the hospital and the acquisition device \citep{zech2018,degrave2021}. Here every SaMi-Trop record is positive and every PTB-XL record negative, and the winning team warned that the original sampling frequency and the mains frequency could act as cues of this kind \citep{vansantvliet2025}. A shortcut also confounds the fine-tuning comparison, because a pooled score favours the model that exploits it best.

We went back to the entry to ask how much more the pretrained encoder had to give. Answering meant first dealing with a property of the public data that we have not seen described: inside CODE-15\%, label prevalence differs by recording length. Section \ref{sec:data} states it, and from there on we compare models within recording length. We fine-tuned the transformer layers in two stages, fed the encoder windows of the length it was pretrained on, added a ranking loss and averaged seeds, one change at a time, each judged by a rule written down before the runs. The organisers scored two of our later entries on the hidden cohorts: a variant built in one day at the Challenge hackathon and the revised entry chosen by this process (section \ref{sec:res-ext}).

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Data and evaluation}
\label{sec:data}
We used the public Challenge training data: CODE-15\% (400 Hz; \citealp{code15data}), SaMi-Trop (400 Hz; \citealp{samitropdata}) and PTB-XL (500 Hz; \citealp{ptbxldata}), \nAll{} records after conversion to the Challenge format. CODE-15\% labels are self-reported, SaMi-Trop labels are serologically confirmed and all positive, and PTB-XL records are presumed negative because of their European origin \citep{reyna2025}. CODE-15\% and PTB-XL contain repeated examinations of the same patient, so we grouped their records by patient (SaMi-Trop records by record) and held out 20\% of the groups, stratified by source and label; no patient appears on both sides of this split. The held-out set has \nTest{} records and \nTestPos{} positives, at the natural prevalence of \testPrev\%. \tpr{} depends on prevalence, so sets of different prevalence are not comparable. The other \nTrain{} records form the training split (table \ref{tab:data}). Sex and age are recorded for every record; \sexFemaleCode\% of CODE-15\%, \sexFemaleSami\% of SaMi-Trop and \sexFemalePtb\% of PTB-XL records are from women. Both were inputs to the original entry and to the first steps of the ablation below, and the final model uses neither. This is a retrospective analysis of public, de-identified data collected under the approvals of the original studies, and no new ethical approval was required.

In CODE-15\%, recording length is associated with the Chagas label. Most recordings are 7.34 s or 10.24 s long, and label prevalence differs by recording length: \prevShort\% of the \nCodeShort{} records shorter than 7.5 s are positive, against \prevLong\% of the \nCodeLong{} records of at least 9.9 s, a ratio of \prevRatio{} (figure \ref{fig:shortcut}(a)). The remaining \nCodeMid{} records, with lengths spread between 7.5 and 9.9 s, include \nCodeMidPos{} positives. Of the CODE-15\% positives, \shareCodePosShort\% are short records. Used alone, record length ranks the held-out CODE-15\% records with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of \durOnlyB. The hidden cohorts are all about 10 s long \citep{reyna2025}. A model cannot use what it learns from length on those cohorts.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_shortcut}
\caption{The length shortcut. (a) Prevalence of the Chagas label in CODE-15\% by record length. (b) Mean predicted probability of held-out CODE-15\% negatives of 7.34 s (circles) and 10.24 s (squares), by model; means over seeds where there are several.}
\label{fig:shortcut}
\end{figure}

We therefore score models within recording length. \emph{S7} is the held-out CODE-15\% records shorter than 7.5 s (\nSseven{} records, \nSsevenPos{} positives); neither length nor source can help there, and it has the most positives. \emph{S10} is the CODE-15\% records of at least 9.9 s (\nSten{} records, \nStenPos{} positives), the format of the hidden cohorts. \emph{S10+}, the mixed-source 10 s set, adds to the negatives of S10 every held-out positive of that length; \nStenPlusPosSami{} of its \nStenPlusPos{} positives are SaMi-Trop records, which adds power but also a source cue, so S10+ matches the hidden cohorts in duration, not in population. View \emph{A}, all held-out records, rewards both cues and is reported for continuity. View \emph{B}, the held-out CODE-15\% records of every length, removes the source cue but keeps the length cue, and view \emph{C} is view A after perturbations of the kinds the organisers describe applying to the hidden data (supplementary note 7). Three diagnostics go with every comparison: the \emph{length-cue gap}, the mean predicted probability of short CODE-15\% negatives minus that of long ones; the mean predicted probability of PTB-XL records, all negative; and the \emph{source gap}, the mean probability of SaMi-Trop positives minus that of CODE-15\% positives.

The primary metric is \tpr; we also report the AUROC, which does not depend on prevalence. Confidence intervals are 95\% percentile intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the held-out records \citep{efron1993}. Two configurations are compared with a paired bootstrap that resamples the same records for both, and we report the standard error (SE) of the difference. The bootstrap resamples records, not patients; repeated examinations of a CODE-15\% patient (\examsPerPatient{} per patient) are not independent, so the SEs are slightly optimistic. The SEs also describe a fixed set of predictions and exclude variation between training seeds. Unless stated otherwise a configuration was trained with three seeds, and we give the mean across them, with the standard deviation across seeds where seed variation matters; a \emph{seed ensemble} averages the three models' probabilities.

\subsection{Model and training}
\label{sec:model}
Figure \ref{fig:pipeline} shows the model. ECG-FM is a convolutional front end followed by 12 transformer layers of width 768, pretrained on 5 s segments sampled at 500 Hz with each lead standardised \citep{mckeen2025}; as in our Challenge entry, we used the released checkpoint that its authors had further fine-tuned on labels from the machine reads of MIMIC-IV-ECG \citep{gow2023}. Leads were put in a fixed order, resampled to 500 Hz, band-pass filtered with a second-order Butterworth filter, as in \citet{hong2025}, notch-filtered at 50 and 60 Hz, and standardised over the record. The cut-offs (0.5 and 45 Hz), the zero-phase application and the two notches are ours. In the baseline the first 10 s of a record form one window, and shorter records are zero-padded at the end.

\label{fig:pipeline}

The classifier wrapper released with ECG-FM detaches the encoder output from the computation graph, so we read the output of each transformer layer with a forward hook. The 12 outputs are combined with learnable softmax weights, initialised to be uniform, and averaged over time; padded positions are left out of the average and masked in the encoder's attention. (In our Challenge entry the mask was dead code, and the zero padding of a 7.34 s record was averaged in as if it were signal.) A head of dropout, a linear layer to 256 units, a rectified linear unit (ReLU), dropout and a linear layer gives one logit. The hooks, layer weights, pooling and head are our own code.

Training has two stages, with the schedule and learning rates of the winning entry \citep{vansantvliet2025}, which in its second stage unfroze all weights, front end included. Stage 1 trains only the layer weights, the demographic network where there is one and the head, for 2,000 optimiser steps at $2\times10^{-4}$ with the encoder frozen. Our stage 2 unfreezes the 12 transformer layers but not the convolutional front end, as in the encoder's own fine-tuning recipe; layer $k$ is trained at $2\times10^{-5}\cdot0.85^{12-k}$ \citep{howard2018} and the head at $10^{-4}$, with a cosine schedule and 5\% warm-up. The batch is 16, accumulated over four batches, in 16-bit mixed precision, with weight decay 0.01 and gradient clipping at 1.0. We kept the checkpoint with the best validation \tpr{} (pooled in rounds 1 and 2, within 7.34 s records in round 3) and stopped after three validations without improvement.

The loss is binary cross-entropy on soft targets with a positive-class weight of 5, which multiplies the positive term only: for target $t$ and predicted probability $p$ the loss is $-[5\,t\log p+(1-t)\log(1-p)]$. Targets are set by source from the record's hard label: 1 for SaMi-Trop, 0 for PTB-XL, and 0.8 or 0.2 for CODE-15\% positives and negatives \citep{vansantvliet2025}. For a CODE-15\% patient with more than one examination, the target is instead $0.51\,y + 0.49\,n_{+}/n$, where $y$ is the record's hard label and $n_{+}/n$ the fraction of the patient's examinations labelled positive \citep{hong2025}; this value replaces the 0.8 or 0.2 rather than being computed from it. The sampler draws records whose hard label is positive five times as often as negatives, and every metric uses the hard label. All positives were used, and negatives were subsampled so that a run saw 100,000 records in total. Baseline wander, Gaussian noise, amplitude scaling, time warping and random masking follow \citet{hong2025}; mains interference and crop-and-shift follow \citet{vansantvliet2025}; resampling to and from another rate and device-like filtering are our own. Every run went through the unmodified Challenge entry scripts, on an NVIDIA Titan RTX with memory capped at 14.5 GiB to mimic the Challenge's 16 GB card (timings in supplementary note 6).

\subsection{Padding, and two interventions on recording length}
\label{sec:length}
In the released checkpoint's configuration (\texttt{extractor\_mode: default}), ECG-FM's front end opens with a group normalisation over time, one group per channel, computed over padded positions as well as real ones, so trailing zeros shift the features at every valid position even when attention masks them (the repository's tests show this for a 7 s record padded to 8 s and to 10 s). Pad every record to 10 s and the shift becomes a fixed function of record length that a head can read off. We tested two interventions.

\textit{Fixed 5 s windows.} ECG-FM was pretrained on 5 s segments \citep{mckeen2025}. Training draws one random 5 s window per record per epoch; validation and testing average the logits of $K=\lceil T/5\,\mathrm{s}\rceil$ evenly spaced windows. Each encoder input then has the same duration and, for records of at least 5 s, contains no trailing padding. The number of windows averaged at inference still differs (two for 7.34 s records, three for 10.24 s), and standardisation is over the whole record, so the prediction as a whole is not blind to duration. Another Challenge team also trained on random 5 s crops and, at inference, averaged the highest quarter of the window scores \citep{dong2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against dong2025 (random 5-s crops in training; top-k averaging across windows, k = 25%; the paper also mentions centred windows at inference).

\textit{Length-matched negatives.} When negatives are subsampled, they are drawn so that their distribution over the three length groups of table \ref{tab:data} equals that of the positives. This removes the association between those groups and the label in the training and validation data, though not every correlate of duration. It is frequency matching of controls to cases on a confounder, the group-balancing remedy for spurious correlations \citep{idrissi2022,sagawa2020}; under the negative cap it changes which negatives are drawn, not how many.

\subsection{Fine-tuning comparison, ranking loss and seed ensembles}
\label{sec:compare}
The fine-tuning comparison sets the stage-2 model of a run against the stage-1 model of the same run, whose encoder is still frozen. For one Challenge team a frozen SEResNet18 encoder beat its fine-tuned version on the hidden validation cohort \citep{wang2025}, and fine-tuning can degrade out-of-distribution performance \citep{kumar2022}, so we also interpolated the weights of the stage-1 model ($\theta_1$) and the stage-2 model ($\theta_2$) as $(1-\alpha)\theta_1+\alpha\theta_2$ \citep{wortsman2022} and scored $\alpha=0$, 0.5 and 1.

The ranking loss is the hard-negative loss of \citet{hong2025}: a margin-ranking loss on the logits of the top 20\% of negatives per batch by predicted probability, with weight 2.5 relative to the cross-entropy and margin 0.5 scaled by the difference of the soft targets of each pair. \Citet{hong2025} scale it by $\max(0.1, c_1-c_2)$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are the soft targets; we floor the difference at 0 instead.

\textit{Seed ensembles} average models that differ only in the random seed \citep{lakshminarayanan2017}, as in earlier Chagas models and one Challenge entry \citep{jidling2023,nejedly2025}. The entry we submitted after the Challenge is a three-seed ensemble.

\subsection{Experimental design}
\label{sec:design}
The work asked three questions in three rounds, each judged by a rule fixed in writing before its runs (table \ref{tab:rules}; supplementary note 1 gives the full texts with their dates and the recipe of every ablation step). Round 1 asked which changes helped our entry. It built the model up from the entry one change at a time (table \ref{tab:ladder}): pipeline corrections, soft labels with class weighting, augmentation, a FiLM-style demographic encoder \citep{perez2018,vansantvliet2025}, stage-2 fine-tuning, removal of age and sex, and a lower band-pass cut-off. These steps (0 to 5c) were single runs. B0, the end of the ladder, is step 5c with the negative cap applied inside the training script, as the organisers would train it, with three seeds; on B0 we also tried stage-2 learning rates of $5\times10^{-6}$ and $10^{-6}$, the latter the rate the authors of ECG-FM used. In rounds 1 and 2, 10\% of the training patients (CODE-15\%) or records (PTB-XL, SaMi-Trop) were held out for validation.

Round 2 asked whether weakening the length cue changed performance within recording length. It trained matched negatives (M1), fixed windows (W1) and both (MW) from B0, three seeds each, and scored MW at the three interpolation weights.

Round 3 asked which configuration to enter, under a fixed validation protocol. Rounds 1 and 2 had selected checkpoints on the pooled validation \tpr, which the length cue inflates, and had carved the validation set after the negative cap using the training seed, so each seed validated on different records. In round 3 the validation set is drawn before the cap, at natural prevalence, from 10\% of the training patients stratified by source, label and length group, with a fixed seed and with PTB-XL grouped by patient. It has \rThreeValN{} records and \rThreeValPos{} positives and is the same for every run. Checkpoints are selected on the validation \tpr{} within 7.34 s CODE-15\% records, which hold \rThreeValPosSseven{} of its positives (\rThreeValPosStenPlus{} are 10 s records). The negative cap becomes a training prevalence of 6.5\%, the value the 100,000-record cap gave on our split, so that it transfers to the organisers' larger training set. The executable entry cannot group PTB-XL by patient, because the organisers' data carry no PTB-XL metadata table, so it groups PTB-XL records individually for its validation split: a PTB-XL patient can straddle the entry's training and validation split, but never the outer held-out split.

Under this protocol we re-trained the baseline and the fixed-window configuration with three seeds. Because these are new models we call them \Bp{} and \Wp. W1 was carried forward instead of MW because the two did not differ on S10+ AUROC by more than one SE in round 2 and W1 is the simpler change with the higher S7 score; length-matched sampling is therefore not part of the entry. We tested three additions to \Wp: the ranking loss (W1R); dropping PTB-XL, which exists only as negatives and is absent from the hidden data (W1S); and inference over 5 s windows every 2.5 s, without retraining. Two further \Wp{} seeds tested a five-seed ensemble. The hidden cohorts are 10 s recordings, so round 3 made the S10+ AUROC its primary metric and kept the S7 \tpr{} as a guard.

The held-out split served as a development set throughout. The written rules document when each decision was made, and a margin of one SE is a selection heuristic, not statistical confirmation; ``qualified'' below means qualified under our rule.

\section{Results}
\subsection{The length--label association, and models that depended on it}
\label{sec:res-entry}
Step 0 of the ladder re-creates our Challenge entry in the new code (supplementary note 6 lists how it differs from the shipped model). It scored \rowZeroA{} in \tpr{} on view A and \rowZeroSseven{} within 7.34 s records (table \ref{tab:ladder}).

\begin{table}
\caption{The ablation ladder, scored on the pooled views and within record-length groups. Steps 0 to 5c are single runs; B0 and the uncapped run are means over seeds.}
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/tab_ladder}}
\label{tab:ladder}
\end{table}

Every model trained on padded 10 s inputs, step 0 included, gave short negatives higher probabilities than long ones. For B0 the mean probability of held-out CODE-15\% negatives was \bzNegShort{} for short records and \bzNegLong{} for long ones, a length-cue gap of \bzGap{} (figure \ref{fig:shortcut}(b)); for step 0 the gap was \rowZeroGap, and for the re-trained baseline \Bp{} of round 3 \rThreeBzGap. Record length alone ranks these records with an AUROC of \durOnlyB, so a pooled score rewards a model for reading it. We noticed this after round 1 had chosen a model to ship: a test written when we rebuilt the pipeline had shown that the padding shift depends on record length, which varied with source, and nine days later we found it varied with the label too. Every comparison below is made within length groups.

\subsection{Fixed windows, matched negatives and the ranking loss}
\label{sec:res-cue}
Both interventions narrowed the length-cue gap in round 2: matched negatives from \bzGap{} to \mOneGap, fixed windows to \wOneGap, and the two together to \mwGap. Fixed windows alone left a gap of \wOneGap{} although every encoder input of a record of at least 5 s was unpadded. That residual is compatible with source or acquisition dependence, a recording device, for example, and with the routes by which duration still reaches the prediction (section \ref{sec:length}); our data do not separate them.

Pooled \tpr{} fell from \bzA{} for B0 to \mOneA{} with matched negatives and \mwA{} with both interventions, consistent with reduced use of the length cue. Within 7.34 s records neither intervention changed \tpr{} by more than its SE (the largest change was \mwDSseven{} $\pm$ \mwDSsevenSe, with both), though fixed windows lifted the AUROC there by \wOneDSsevenAuc{} $\pm$ \wOneDSsevenAucSe. Fixed windows raised the S10+ AUROC by \wOneDStenPlusAuc{} $\pm$ \wOneDStenPlusAucSe; matched negatives, which leave the input untouched, gained \mOneDStenPlusAuc{} $\pm$ \mOneDStenPlusAucSe, and the two together \mwDStenPlusAuc{} $\pm$ \mwDStenPlusAucSe. On S10, which has no SaMi-Trop records but only \nStenPos{} positives, the AUROC was \bzStenAuc{} for B0 and \mwStenAuc{} with both interventions. By the rule we had written down beforehand, none of this was enough to adopt anything (supplementary note 4 gives all of round 2).

The fixed protocol of round 3 changed little by itself: \Bp{} scored \rThreeBzSseven{} within short records and \rThreeBzStenPlusAuc{} in S10+ AUROC, close to B0 in round 2 (table \ref{tab:round3}). \Wp{} again left S7 where it was (\rThreeWoneDSseven) and raised the S10+ AUROC by \rThreeWoneDStenPlusAuc; with S10+ primary, that qualified. All three additions qualified against \Bp, but none beat \Wp{} on S10+ by more than one SE. Overlapping windows changed nothing, and dropping PTB-XL did not make the positives more separable by source. On the S7 score the ranking loss gained \rThreeWoneRVsWoneDSseven{} over \Wp{} without losing on S10+, which qualified it under the second clause of the rule, and W1R became the entry, although its margin was only \rThreeWoneRVsWoneNse{} SE. We also took into account that the length-cue gap fell from \rThreeWoneGap{} for \Wp{} to \rThreeWoneRGap. On S10 the AUROC was \rThreeBzStenAuc{} for \Bp, \rThreeWoneStenAuc{} for \Wp{} and \rThreeWoneRStenAuc{} for W1R, a difference from \Bp{} of \rThreeWoneRDStenAuc; with so few positives the uncertainty is wide, but the direction matches S10+.

\subsection{Stage 2 against stage 1}
\label{sec:res-ft}
After both length-cue interventions, stage 2 improved performance over the stage-1 checkpoint. In the round-2 configuration with both interventions the stage-1 model ($\alpha=0$, encoder frozen) scored \frozenSseven{} within 7.34 s records and the fine-tuned model ($\alpha=1$) \mwSseven, all three seeds moving the same way, and the AUROC followed: \frozenSsevenAuc{} and \mwSsevenAuc{} within 7.34 s records, \frozenStenPlusAuc{} and \mwStenPlusAuc{} on S10+ (table \ref{tab:alpha}). Halfway interpolation ($\alpha=0.5$) scored \halfSseven, below the \mwSseven{} obtained with full fine-tuning, so we retained full fine-tuning.

\begin{table}
\caption{Stage 2 against stage 1 (round 2, three seeds). ``Both interventions'' is fixed 5 s windows with length-matched negatives; $\alpha$ interpolates the weights between the stage-1 model of each run ($\alpha=0$, encoder frozen) and its fine-tuned model ($\alpha=1$). $\Delta$ is the difference from the baseline mean, with the SE of a paired bootstrap. Supplementary note 4 gives all of round 2.}
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/tab_alpha}}
\label{tab:alpha}
\end{table}

The frozen arm is the stage-1 model of the same run, a head trained for 2,000 steps, not a frozen encoder trained until it stopped improving. Step 0, a frozen encoder with a head trained for 16 epochs, is nearer the latter---it differs from B0 in other ways too, and it is a single run---and within 7.34 s records it scored \rowZeroSseven{} against \bzSseven{} for the fine-tuned B0, a difference we cannot tell from noise. The comparison the question needs, continued head-only training against unfreezing under the same pipeline, budget and checkpoint rule across seeds, we did not run. Stage 2 improves on stage 1; whether a fine-tuned ECG-FM beats a frozen one trained to convergence, our data do not show.

At the base learning rate, stage-2 performance peaked within the first two epochs. For the three B0 seeds the checkpoint selected on pooled validation \tpr{} came from epoch \bestEpHighMax{} at the latest (mean \bestEpHigh), and the validation AUROC plotted in supplementary figure S1 also peaked by epoch \aucPeakEpHighMax{} and then declined (supplementary note 2). Lower rates delayed the selected checkpoint (mean epoch \bestEpLow{} at $10^{-6}$) but did not raise the best validation \tpr, and test \tpr{} fell as the rate fell (\lrLowSseven{} within 7.34 s records, against \bzSseven{} at the base rate), so we kept $2\times10^{-5}$. Training on all negatives rather than a capped third was worse under this schedule: the AUROC within short records fell to \fullSsevenAuc{} (B0: \bzSsevenAuc), and validating every 500 steps, so as not to miss the early peak on the larger set, did not recover it. We do not generalise this; every later configuration kept the cap. The learned layer weights, which stayed near uniform once the encoder was fine-tuned, are described in supplementary note 3.

\subsection{The ablation ladder}
\label{sec:res-ladder}
The ladder's main lesson is that pooled and within-length rankings differ (table \ref{tab:ladder}). Ranked by pooled score, step 1 is best; ranked within 7.34 s records, the steps without age and sex are. Each step was a single run and the bootstrap SE of \tpr{} in S7 is about \seSsevenTpr, so most differences between neighbouring rows are noise. Removing age and sex (step 5 to 5b) produced the largest increase in S7 \tpr: \demoDropDSseven, approximately \demoDropNse{} SE. No step changed the score by two SE. Two steps moved the diagnostics more than the score. Soft labels and class weighting halved the length-cue gap (\rowOneGap{} at step 1, \rowTwoGap{} at step 2), and augmentation raised the mean probability of PTB-XL records from \ptbRowTwo{} to \ptbRowThree, as would be expected if resampling every record to and from other rates hides the 500 Hz sampling of PTB-XL. The demographic input pulled that mean the other way: to \ptbRowFour{} with the FiLM-style encoder of step 4, and to \ptbRowFive{} once the encoder was fine-tuned with age and sex still fed in. PTB-XL is an all-negative European cohort with its own age and sex distribution, so a mean of \ptbRowFive{} is consistent with source or acquisition dependence, though it does not identify it. Removing age and sex raised the value to \ptbRowFiveB{} without lowering the score within length groups, and the final model uses neither.

\subsection{Seed ensembles}
\label{sec:res-ens}
The most dependable gain in the study came from averaging three seeds. The baseline's \tpr{} within short records went from \bzSseven{} to \bzEnsSseven{} and its AUROC there from \bzSsevenAuc{} to \bzEnsSsevenAuc, about as much as the largest step of the ladder, and without resting on a single run. The ensembles also carried the fixed-window advantage on S10+: \wOneEnsStenPlusAuc{} and \mwEnsStenPlusAuc{} in AUROC for fixed windows and the combined configuration, against \bzEnsStenPlusAuc{} for the baseline ensemble. The W1R ensemble reached \rThreeWoneREnsSseven{} on S7, the highest S7 score of any ensemble in rounds 1 to 3, \rThreeWoneREnsStenPlusAuc{} in S10+ AUROC and \rThreeWoneREnsStenAuc{} on S10. Five \Wp{} seeds gained \rThreeWfiveVsWoneDEnsStenPlusAuc{} over three on S10+, which gave us no reason to train more members.

The post-Challenge entry is the three members of W1R trained inside a single call of the Challenge training script. It scored \entrySseven{} on S7 (AUROC \entrySsevenAuc), \entryStenPlusAuc{} in AUROC on S10+ and \entryStenAuc{} on S10, within the confidence interval of the round-3 W1R ensemble.

The test mean of the post-Challenge entry rose by \extDeltaMean{} over the original, all of it on two cohorts: REDS-II gained \extDeltaReds{} and SaMi-Trop 3 \extDeltaSami.

The hackathon entry was built in one day at the Challenge hackathon, held on 14 September 2025 in S\~ao Paulo during Computing in Cardiology 2025, with entries due that night (commit fa155fb). It was the entry with the powerline-interference and crop-and-shift augmentations, class weighting and a FiLM-style demographic encoder: the frozen-encoder Challenge entry with synthetic mains interference at 50 or 60 Hz and its harmonics added to half the records, random crop-and-shift of every record, a positive-class weight of 5 with five-fold oversampling of positives, and age and sex fed through a FiLM-style encoder, trained with hard labels for 11 epochs on the entire recording. It scored \extHackMean{} on the test cohorts, third of the eleven hackathon entries scored \citep{physionet2025hackathon}, below the original entry's \extOrigMean, and \extHackVal{} on hidden validation. That is in line with the ladder's later finding that FiLM, class weighting and augmentation on a frozen encoder gave no gain within recording length (steps 2 to 4, table \ref{tab:ladder}), but it is one externally scored configuration, built in a day, with hard labels where the ladder used soft ones and with only part of the ladder's augmentation.

ELSA-Brasil is the cohort where we understand the result least. The original and post-Challenge entries scored \extNewElsa{} there, and so did the winning entry \citep{physionet2025results}; the hackathon entry scored \extHackElsa. The metric takes few distinct values on that cohort but is not fixed at one, and identical scores do not distinguish the original and post-Challenge entries there. The post-Challenge entry's AUROC of \extNewElsaAuc{} on ELSA-Brasil (hackathon entry \extHackElsaAuc) indicates limited discrimination, whatever the resolution of \tpr.

For context, the highest official test mean was 0.323 (REDS-II 0.468, SaMi-Trop 3 0.376, ELSA-Brasil 0.125), the second 0.283 and the median of the ranked entries 0.217 \citep{reyna2025,physionet2025results}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against the official results table (challenge_2025_results.tsv: top 0.323 = 0.468 / 0.376 / 0.125; second 0.283; median over the 39 ranked rows 0.217).
A score of \extNewMean{} would sit between the first and the second, but an entry submitted after the Challenge closed is not ranked, and it was built with the published methods of other teams.

\section{Discussion}
\subsection{Fine-tuning ECG-FM}
During the Challenge we interpreted our result as fine-tuning overwriting what pretraining had taught the encoder. That evidence was one pooled comparison with single-stage fine-tuning, on data where every model trained on padded 10 s inputs scored short negatives higher, and we did not re-run it. Measured within recording length, a short second stage improved on the stage-1 checkpoint, in the direction the winning team and the authors of ECG-FM had found \citep{vansantvliet2025,mckeen2025}, and it did so early; against a frozen encoder trained to convergence the question remains open (section \ref{sec:res-ft}). We also expected a lower learning rate and more negatives to help; neither did under our schedule. If we were starting again on a task like this one, we would run stage 2 at a base rate near $2\times10^{-5}$, not the $10^{-6}$ its authors used, validate often enough to catch a peak inside the first two epochs, and keep a cap on the negatives until it had been tested on the task at hand.

The input and the head told us less about the encoder than we had hoped. Fixed 5 s windows do three things at once: they give ECG-FM the segment length it was pretrained on, they remove the padding that the group normalisation turns into a length signature, and they present every record of at least 5 s to the encoder as unpadded inputs of one duration. We cannot apportion the gain among the three. Matched negatives, which touch none of the input, also gained on S10+, so part of what the windows gained may come from weakening the length association rather than from the input format. We added the ranking loss because it targets the top of the ranking, which determines the Challenge score, and had been used by \citet{hong2025}. It also reduced the residual length-cue gap after windowing. Our guess at the mechanism is that, with the length association in place, the negatives scored highest in a batch are disproportionately short records, so a loss that pushes them below the positives also pushes down the format signal; we never tabulated the lengths of the negatives it selected. Age and sex we would leave out. With fine-tuning they let the model pick out PTB-XL records without finding more Chagas, and the winning team's FiLM-style scale and shift from a demographic encoder \citep{vansantvliet2025} need not contradict that: in our ladder FiLM helped the pooled score only while the encoder was frozen, and a frozen or differently trained encoder might still gain from it.

\subsection{The shortcut, and what it means for anyone using CODE-15\%}
Our internal and hidden scores were not the only ones to disagree. Across the 65 teams whose entries were scored, the median score fell from 0.279 on the hidden validation cohort to 0.236 and 0.100 on two of the test cohorts \citep{reyna2025}, and one team watched a variant gain 0.20 locally and lose 0.11 on hidden validation \citep{wang2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against reyna2025 (medians over the 65 scored teams: 0.279 REDS-II validation, 0.236 SaMi-Trop 3, 0.100 ELSA-Brasil; best 0.323) and wang2025 table 1 (ECGNeXt 0.827 local, 0.230 validation; frozen SEResNet18 0.627 local, 0.338 validation).
We do not know why record length is associated with the label. The two lengths may correspond to two recording systems or software versions in the telehealth network that collected CODE-15\% \citep{ribeiro2020}, deployed in regions or periods with different prevalence of Chagas disease, which would also fit the residual gap of models whose encoder inputs carry no padding. The public data carry no device or site information, so we could not test this. Pooled and within-length AUROC differ for every ladder step (supplementary note 5), but they are computed on different records and do not measure how much the length association added to any score, here or in the gap between internal and hidden scores. Two of the three highest-ranked entries used augmentations that blur the association. The winning team cropped records at random to between 5.65 and 10 s and zero-padded them \citep{vansantvliet2025}, and the third-placed team masked the beginning and end of records ``to simulate shorter signals'' \citep{hong2025}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against vansantvliet2025 (table 1: crop L1 in [5.65, 10] s; zero-padded to 10 s) and hong2025 (3rd of 41; "to simulate shorter signals").
Neither team described the association with the label. In our own Challenge paper we listed random padding or windowing as future work \citep{nguyen2025}.

For anyone working with CODE-15\%, the practical point is that a pooled score cannot rank models. From step 0 to B0 the pooled \tpr{} rose from \rowZeroA{} to \bzA{} while the score within 7.34 s records stayed within noise (\rowZeroSseven{} and \bzSseven), and the patient-grouped split at natural prevalence, both of which we consider necessary, did nothing to prevent it. We suggest scoring 7.34 s and 10.24 s records separately, reporting the duration-only baseline and the length-cue gap, and expecting pooled scores to fall when the length association is weakened. Length-matched sampling changes which negatives are drawn, not how many, so it is cheap where negatives are plentiful. Neither it nor fixed windows guarantees that a model is blind to duration. For ECG-FM, we recommend evaluating its pretraining format of 5 s at 500 Hz and checking how the front end handles padding. Had we known about the length association at the start, we would have scored within format from the first run, and we would not have spent a round ranking changes by a pooled score that the length association was moving.

\subsection{What the hidden scores can and cannot show}
The post-Challenge entry, trained by the organisers with the unmodified entry scripts, found more positives among its top 5\% than our original entry on two of the three hidden test cohorts, in the direction the within-format evidence predicted. Every hidden AUROC was below the \entryStenPlusAuc{} the entry reached on S10+ of our held-out set, the lowest being \extNewElsaAuc{} on ELSA-Brasil. That was to be expected: the held-out set chose the entry, and the hidden cohorts are a different population with serological labels and their own devices. An earlier network reached 0.68 and 0.59 on its own versions of REDS-II and ELSA-Brasil \citep{jidling2023}.
% verified 2026-11-12 against jidling2023 (abstract: AUROC 0.68 REDS-II, 0.59 ELSA-Brasil).

The external comparison evaluates the complete revised pipeline and cannot identify the contribution of each change. Between the original and the revised entry sit the pipeline corrections, soft labels, augmentation, the removal of age and sex, fine-tuning, fixed windows, the ranking loss, the validation protocol and the ensemble, and the hidden score tests the lot as a package; the hackathon entry, too, differs from the original by several changes at once. Whether fine-tuning alone would have moved REDS-II, or whether dropping age and sex mattered there, can only be settled by a scored entry that differs by one change. Without confidence intervals from the organisers we cannot say how much of the difference is sampling variation either. For scale, the bootstrap SE of \tpr{} on our 7.34 s held-out records was about \seSsevenTpr.

Internally, the 10 s data of our held-out set are thin: \nStenPos{} CODE-15\% positives, and most of the positives in S10+ are SaMi-Trop records, which a model may recognise by source rather than by disease; the round-3 gain also appeared on S10 alone, but with wide uncertainty. The held-out split was the selection set for every decision in three rounds, so the entry's internal scores are optimistic, and the round-3 rule, though fixed before its runs, was written after round 2 had shown the 10 s-format gain. Our SEs come from a record-level bootstrap of fixed predictions, so they ignore the correlation between a patient's examinations and the variation between training seeds. Length-matched sampling was not re-tested under the fixed protocol. Other limitations are typical of a single study: one split, one backbone, no comparator without a foundation-model encoder, single runs on the ladder before B0, self-reported labels in the largest source, and no results stratified by sex.

\section{Conclusion}
We went back to a frozen-encoder entry to ask how much more ECG-FM had to give, and found that measuring the answer needed most of the effort. A short second stage of fine-tuning at a moderate learning rate, unpadded windows of the length the encoder was pretrained on, a ranking loss and an ensemble of three seeds made an entry that the organisers scored higher than our original one. On CODE-15\%, comparisons should include results within recording-length groups because pooled performance can favour models that exploit the association between length and label.
